mainEntity.name: What IFR personal minimums should a new instrument pilot use?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single FAA set. Start from the lowest IFR conditions you have recently and regularly flown with comfort, then add margin for night, fatigue, an unfamiliar airport or a long layoff. As one example, the Risk Management Handbook’s sample pilot uses 800 ft and 1 mile by day and 999 ft and 3 miles at night.

mainEntity.name: Is being IFR current the same as being proficient?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Currency under 14 CFR 61.57(c) is six approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking courses within the 6 calendar months before the month of the flight. The Risk Management Handbook notes that a current pilot may still lack proficiency if those events were months ago, and its example pilot adds 500 ft to her approach minimums for that reason.

mainEntity.name: Should I use different minimums for an ILS and an RNAV (GPS) approach?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many pilots do. The FAA checklist has separate lines for precision and non-precision approaches, and the Instrument Procedures Handbook classifies approaches with vertical guidance, such as LPV and LNAV/VNAV, as non-precision. Decide which column your vertically guided approaches use and keep it consistent.

mainEntity.name: When can I lower my IFR personal minimums?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only after a significant positive event, and never while planning a specific flight. Change one variable at a time, and get training or talk to a flight instructor before a significant change. Making minimums more restrictive is fine at any time.

mainEntity.name: What are the legal IFR alternate requirements?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under 14 CFR 91.169 you need an alternate unless the destination has an instrument approach and, from 1 hour before to 1 hour after your ETA, the forecast is at least a 2,000 ft ceiling and 3 statute miles. The alternate must forecast its published alternate minimums, or 600 ft and 2 statute miles for a precision approach and 800 ft and 2 statute miles for a non-precision approach.

mainEntity.name: Should a low-time instrument pilot fly in icing or near thunderstorms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not in an airplane without known-icing approval, and not into clouds with embedded thunderstorms without detection equipment. The Instrument Flying Handbook warns that structural icing can only get worse. Write these as yes-or-no rules, not numbers to stretch.
